passages.t: ‘I will walk in my house with integrity of heart’: a ruler's promise
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of David” (verse 1). It is a promise, spoken to God by someone with power. “I will sing of Your loving devotion and justice; to You, O LORD, I will sing praises” (verse 1).

He starts with himself. “I will ponder the way that is blameless” (verse 2). Then a sudden question: ‘when will You come to me?’ “I will walk in my house with integrity of heart” (verse 2). “I will set no worthless thing before my eyes” (verse 3).

Then he speaks of the people around him. “Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret, I will put to silence; the one with haughty eyes and a proud heart, I will not endure” (verse 5). He wants faithful people near him (verse 6). “No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who tells lies shall stand in my presence” (verse 7).

It ends with a daily duty. “Every morning I will remove all the wicked of the land” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Many readers take this as a king's vow, perhaps made when he was crowned. It is a royal psalm, as the book page notes. A king in that world was surrounded by people seeking favour. Whispered slander and flattery were the ordinary tools of a royal court, as the stories of Saul and David show. The king here promises to shut his door to them.

Rulers in the ancient world often boasted that they were just. What is different here is where the king begins. Before he speaks of anyone else's behaviour, he speaks of his own heart, his own eyes and his own house.

‘Every morning’ (verse 8) fits what the prophets asked of Judah's kings: “Administer justice every morning” (Jeremiah 21:12). Justice was to be daily work, not a rare event.

Notice the question in verse 2: ‘when will You come to me?’ The king knows that he cannot keep this vow alone. He needs God near.
passages.later:
Jesus warned against judging others first: “Why do you look at the speck in your brother's eye, but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3). Psalm 101 begins with the king's own eye.

Paul says a leader in the church “must be above reproach” (1 Timothy 3:2). And he tells every believer what to set before the mind: “whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure” (Philippians 4:8).
passages.hard: Does verse 8 describe a harsh ruler who silences anyone he dislikes? The people it names are slanderers, the proud, liars and the wicked who prey on others. It is the king's duty to protect the weak from them. But this is a king's vow, under God and in God's city, and the psalm gives no one today the right to punish neighbours on their own. Its first demand falls on the ruler himself.
passages.asks:
You may not be a king, but you have a ‘house’: a home, a workplace, a set of friends, a screen. What do you set before your eyes there (verse 3)? What talk do you allow (verse 5)?

Begin where the psalm begins, with your own heart. Then pray its question: ‘When will You come to me?’ Integrity is not something we build alone.
